Metabolic Roles of Nucleotides
The most abundant ribonucleotide in the body is adenosine 5′–triphosphate (ATP), which is the universal energy carrier in living
organisms (Figure 1(b)). In addition, nucleotides are precursors of several coenzymes, used in many reactions including the conver-
sion of food into energy. Within cells adenosine and guanosine nucleotides also have roles in the transduction of external signals
into cellular responses, and in the translation and synthesis of proteins. Pyrimidine nucleotides are present at much lower concen-
trations in cells but also fulﬁll diverse functions. Uridine diphosphate (UDP)-glucose and Cytidine diphosphate (CDP)-lipids are
active intermediates in the synthesis of glycogen and membranes, respectively, and sugars linked to UDP or GDP are used in the
glycosylation of proteins. UDP-glucuronic acid is an essential component of the pathways that convert exogenous molecules
and endogenous steroids into soluble forms for disposal from the body.
The free deoxyribonucleotides are very scarce in the normal cell because they are used exclusively for the synthesis of DNA.
